content:
Earlier this year, when Apple launched the MacBook Neo, the personal computer market was clearly caught off-guard. Although the aggressive pricing strategy of that notebook was later adjusted according to market conditions, the Windows camp's rivals took several months to gradually reveal their counterattack products. HP joined the fray today, launching a brand new notebook equipped with an OLED screen, also priced from $699 — however, there are quite a few limitations behind this price.

Overall, the HP OmniBook 5 14 looks like a colourful budget version of the MacBook Neo body, complemented by the more refined, understated green and blue tones of the Apple iPad Air series. Underneath the 14-inch screen, the body is only 11.77mm thick and weighs just 2.56 pounds — although it's perfect for back-to-school shopping, HP somehow missed this window for some reason. The real highlight of this machine is that 14-inch screen — at this price point you'd normally only see an IPS panel, but this time two OLED options are offered for you to choose from, with detailed specifications to be announced later. Each side of the body has a full-function USB-C port and a headphone jack; lifting open the screen reveals an FHD camera that supports Windows Hello.

In terms of hardware specifications, HP stated that this notebook can support up to an Intel Core 7 processor, but the model on display only came in a single configuration. The battery life on the spec sheet is quite impressive — up to 42 hours of local video playback (battery capacity not listed) — however, in fairness, local video playback tests may not reflect real-world usage. HP mentioned that this machine is compatible with its 65W GaN mini charger, which is expected to be included in the box. Beyond that, known specs include dual microphones and audio tuned by Poly Studio; if you feel there's still a lot of information missing, you're certainly not the only one who feels this way.

Firstly, the processor model of the $700 version of this notebook has still not been announced, making it hard to stack up directly against Apple's A18 Pro. HP also chose not to disclose any storage space or memory configuration information — not even the 'maximum' figures — which directly reflects the immense pressure facing the PC market amid the current tight memory supply. Even the most striking selling point comes with a fatal trade-off: HP spent quite a bit of time at the launch event detailing that 2.5K OLED screen, but that version won't ship until March 2027. The model going on sale at Best Buy later this month comes with a 2K OLED screen, but the luminance drops from 650 nits all the way down to a mere 300 nits.

Given all the above unlisted details, and some disappointing answers, if HP has still managed to pique your interest, please keep a close eye on more information to be released before the product officially goes on sale.
